title: Transactional Migrations and Rollback Planning
learningObjectives: Explain how a transaction can make a migration atomic.
Group related schema and data changes inside a transaction where supported.
Demonstrate rollback of an uncommitted SQLite schema change.
Recognize DBMS-specific DDL transaction and implicit-commit behaviour.
Plan backups and recovery for changes that cannot be safely reversed.

understand.concept: A migration may include multiple dependent schema and data changes. Where supported, a transaction can make the migration atomic: all included changes commit together or are rolled back together. Some DBMS products implicitly commit certain DDL statements, so behaviour must be checked per engine.
understand.whyItMatters: Rollback planning protects data and application availability when a deployment encounters a failed migration step.
understand.analogy: A migration is like a numbered building renovation plan: each change has a recorded step, a verification and a recovery plan.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy does not model transactional DDL, locking, data backfills, version checks or application compatibility.

explain.narrative:
## Transactional migration
A migration can begin a transaction, apply schema changes, backfill data, update the migration history and commit only after all checks pass. If a required step fails, roll back the uncommitted work.

## DDL portability
SQLite supports transactional schema changes in many cases. Other products have different DDL transaction rules; some statements implicitly commit or cannot be rolled back. Never assume a migration transaction behaves identically across DBMS products.

## Recovery planning
A rollback script is not always the reverse of a forward migration. Dropping a newly added column can lose data written after deployment. Prefer forward-compatible changes, backups and tested recovery procedures.

### Transactional DDL is product-specific
A migration may combine schema and data changes, but whether DDL participates in a transaction depends on the DBMS and the particular command. SQLite supports transactional schema changes for the demonstrated ALTER TABLE operation. Other engines may implicitly commit, restrict, or otherwise handle DDL differently.

### Rollback planning
A rollback plan should state whether the reverse change is safe, whether data loss is possible, and how application versions remain compatible. For destructive schema changes, a forward-fix migration is often safer than attempting to reconstruct dropped data.

examples.title: Create an account table
examples.code: CREATE TABLE mig18_accounts (account_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, balance INTEGER NOT NULL);
examples.explanation: Creates the account table used to demonstrate a transactional schema change. The balance is stored as an integer for this fixture; real systems must define currency precision and units explicitly.

examples.title: Insert a starting balance
examples.explanation: Inserts one account with a starting balance. This row is used to verify that rollback preserves the original data.

examples.title: Begin a migration and add a temporary column
examples.code: BEGIN; ALTER TABLE mig18_accounts ADD COLUMN note TEXT; UPDATE mig18_accounts SET note = 'migration candidate';
examples.explanation: Begins a transaction, adds a nullable note column and updates the row. These changes remain uncommitted so the next statement can demonstrate rollback of both schema and data changes in SQLite.

examples.title: Roll back the uncommitted migration
examples.explanation: Rolls back the open transaction. In SQLite, this example's transactional ALTER TABLE change is rolled back along with the update; DDL transaction guarantees differ across DBMS products and operations.

examples.title: Verify the column and original row remain unchanged
examples.code: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM pragma_table_info('mig18_accounts') WHERE name = 'note'; SELECT balance FROM mig18_accounts WHERE account_id = 1;
examples.explanation: Inspects pragma_table_info to confirm the note column is absent, then reads the original balance. The expected output verifies that both the schema change and data update were undone.

practise.guidedTask: Run the examples and verify that rollback removes the uncommitted column and preserves the original balance.
practise.independentTask: Design a migration with two schema changes and a data backfill. Identify which steps can be rolled back in your target DBMS and what recovery plan is needed if a later step fails.
hints: Start the transaction before the related schema and data changes.
Commit only after all required checks pass.
SQLite supports transactional DDL for many schema operations.
Check implicit commit rules in MySQL, SQL Server, PostgreSQL and other targets.
A rollback script may not recover data written after deployment; plan backups and forward fixes.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of a transactional migration?
options: To commit related schema and data changes together or roll them back
To run SQL without a database
questions.answer: To commit related schema and data changes together or roll them back
questions.explanation: A transaction can make a group of migration steps atomic when the engine supports it.

questions.prompt: Can all DBMS products roll back every DDL statement?
options: No, DDL transaction rules differ by product and statement
questions.answer: No, DDL transaction rules differ by product and statement
questions.explanation: Some products implicitly commit certain DDL operations or have other limitations.

options: After all required changes and checks succeed
Only when a SELECT returns NULL
questions.answer: After all required changes and checks succeed
questions.explanation: Commit only when the migration is complete and verified.

questions.prompt: Why is a rollback script not always a simple reverse operation?
options: New data may have been written after deployment and could be lost
SQL statements cannot be reversed alphabetically
questions.answer: New data may have been written after deployment and could be lost
questions.explanation: Reversing a deployed change may destroy new data or require a compensating forward migration.

questions.prompt: What should accompany a risky production migration?
options: A tested backup and recovery plan
Only a new SQL editor theme
questions.answer: A tested backup and recovery plan
questions.explanation: Backups and recovery planning reduce risk if the migration fails.
